```{r results-setup, include=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(flextable)
library(scales)

# Resolve the project root whether this file is rendered standalone or via the
# full project (where _quarto.yml sets `execute: dir: project`).
# When rendered standalone, getwd() returns the file's own directory; we walk
# up until we find _quarto.yml to locate the actual project root.
.find_root <- function(start = getwd()) {
  path <- normalizePath(start, winslash = "/")
  while (!file.exists(file.path(path, "_quarto.yml"))) {
    parent <- normalizePath(dirname(path), winslash = "/")
    if (parent == path) stop("Could not find project root (_quarto.yml)")
    path <- parent
  }
  path
}
.root <- .find_root()
.p <- function(...) file.path(.root, ...)

rep     <- read.csv(.p("results/11_repeatability/repeatability_summary.csv"))
pred    <- read.csv(.p("results/12_predictability/predictability_summary.csv"))
clust   <- read.csv(.p("results/14_individual_traits/behaviour_clusters.csv"))
mcomp   <- read.csv(.p("results/15_pca_clustering/method_comparison.csv"))
k_m3    <- read.csv(.p("results/15_pca_clustering/pca_M3_c1_int_k_stability.csv"))
load_m3 <- read.csv(.p("results/15_pca_clustering/pca_M3_c1_int_loadings.csv"))

# ── Format helpers ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(round(x, digits), format = "f", digits = digits)
fmt_ci <- function(m, l, u, digits = 2) {
  sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", fmt(m, digits), fmt(l, digits), fmt(u, digits))
}

# Repeatability
r_val  <- function(v) fmt(rep$R_cow_mean[rep$variable == v])
r_ci   <- function(v) paste0("[", fmt(rep$R_cow_lower[rep$variable == v]), ", ",
                                   fmt(rep$R_cow_upper[rep$variable == v]), "]")

# CVi
cvi_val <- function(v) fmt(rep$CVi_mean[rep$variable == v])
cvi_ci  <- function(v) paste0("[", fmt(rep$CVi_lower[rep$variable == v]), ", ",
                                    fmt(rep$CVi_upper[rep$variable == v]), "]")

# CVP
cvp_val <- function(v) fmt(pred$CVP_mean[pred$variable == v])
cvp_ci  <- function(v) paste0("[", fmt(pred$CVP_lower[pred$variable == v]), ", ",
                                    fmt(pred$CVP_upper[pred$variable == v]), "]")

# rIIV
riiv_val <- function(v) fmt(pred$rIIV_mean[pred$variable == v])
riiv_ci  <- function(v) paste0("[", fmt(pred$rIIV_lower[pred$variable == v]), ", ",
                                     fmt(pred$rIIV_upper[pred$variable == v]), "]")

# ── Behavior clusters ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
clean_label <- function(v) gsub("_", " ", v)

c1_vars <- clust$variable[clust$cluster == 1]
c2_vars <- clust$variable[clust$cluster == 2]
c3_vars <- clust$variable[clust$cluster == 3]

# ── PCA / clustering metrics (pulled from the precomputed comparison table) ────
m3        <- mcomp[mcomp$method == "M3_c1_int", ]
m3_sil    <- fmt(m3$mean_sil)
m3_ncomp  <- m3$n_comp
m3_cumvar <- m3$cum_var_pct
m3_k      <- m3$optimal_k
m3_rc1    <- m3$var_rc1_pct
m3_rc2    <- m3$var_rc2_pct

# Parse and sort cluster sizes (largest to smallest)
m3_sizes <- sort(as.integer(strsplit(m3$cluster_sizes, "/")[[1]]), decreasing = TRUE)
n_cows   <- sum(m3_sizes)
m3_pct   <- function(i) round(m3_sizes[i] / n_cows * 100)

# K stability
m3_k_wins  <- k_m3$wins[k_m3$k == m3_k]
m3_k_total <- sum(k_m3$wins)
```

# 4. Results

Throughout this section, all repeatability and predictability measures (R, CVi, CVP, and rIIV) are reported as posterior means followed by their 95% credible intervals (CrIs) in square brackets.

## 4.1 Among-Individual Variation: Repeatability and CVi


Because R is confounded by within-individual variance (Section 3.4), we use the coefficient of individual variation (CVi) as the primary metric for comparing the magnitude of among-individual differences across the 16 behavioral variables, and we report R alongside CVi as a reference for how reliably those differences persist from day to day (Table 1, @fig-rep-cvp-scatter).

Among all variables, the total number of non-nutritive visits showed the largest relative among-individual variation (CVi = `r cvi_val("number_of_non_nutritive_visits")` `r cvi_ci("number_of_non_nutritive_visits")`), meaning that on average, cows differ from one another by more than half the population mean in how often they visit a feed bin without eating. The total number of actor events (CVi = `r cvi_val("total_actor")` `r cvi_ci("total_actor")`) and the median number of non-nutritive visits per meal (CVi = `r cvi_val("median_non_nutritive_per_meal")` `r cvi_ci("median_non_nutritive_per_meal")`) were also highly variable across individuals, indicating that agonistic and non-nutritive visiting frequencies are the most individually distinguishing behaviors in this herd among all variables we evalauted. At the other end of the spectrum, the percentage of meal time spent actively feeding (CVi = `r cvi_val("median_feeding_pct_per_meal")` `r cvi_ci("median_feeding_pct_per_meal")`) and daily feed intake (CVi = `r cvi_val("feed_intake")` `r cvi_ci("feed_intake")`) showed the smallest relative variation, meaning cows are nearly indistinguishable from one another on these dimensions.

Repeatability (R) provides complementary but not redundant information. Daily water drinking duration had the highest R (`r r_val("water_duration")` `r r_ci("water_duration")`), followed by daily feeding visits (R = `r r_val("feed_visits")` `r r_ci("feed_visits")`) and the total number of non-nutritive visits (R = `r r_val("number_of_non_nutritive_visits")` `r r_ci("number_of_non_nutritive_visits")`). The lowest R values were observed for the median proportion of feed remaining when a cow arrived at a bin (R = `r r_val("median_pct_feed_remaining")` `r r_ci("median_pct_feed_remaining")`), median feed intake per meal (R = `r r_val("median_intake_per_meal")` `r r_ci("median_intake_per_meal")`), and median meal duration (R = `r r_val("median_meal_duration")` `r r_ci("median_meal_duration")`).

As articulated in Section 3.4, R and CVi do not always rank traits the same way. The clearest example is the median percentage of meal time spent feeding, which has a moderately high R (`r r_val("median_feeding_pct_per_meal")` `r r_ci("median_feeding_pct_per_meal")`) but the lowest CVi of all 16 variables (`r cvi_val("median_feeding_pct_per_meal")` `r cvi_ci("median_feeding_pct_per_meal")`). The high R values are not driven by high among-individual variation, instead it is driven by the low within-individual variance. In other words, each cow is very consistent within themselves from day to day, so R ($R = \frac{\text{var.cow}}{\text{var.cow} + \text{var.res}}$) is inflated by low residual (within-individual) variance rather than by high among-individual variance. Variables ranked near the top on both R and CVi (e.g., the total number of non-nutritive visits, water drinking duration), represent the most useful candidates for individual profiling, since cows both differ meaningfully from one another and behave consistently enough for those differences to be detectable from repeated observations.

# Pretty variable labels and category grouping. Note: "Median % feed remaining"
# is grouped under "Feeding" (it describes the state of the feed bin the cow
# chose, not a non-nutritive behavior).
var_meta <- tibble::tribble(
  ~variable,                          ~Category,              ~Variable,
  "feed_intake",                      "Feeding",              "Daily feed intake",
  "feed_duration",                    "Feeding",              "Daily feeding duration",
  "feed_visits",                      "Feeding",              "Daily feeding visits",
  "median_pct_feed_remaining",        "Feeding",              "Median % feed remaining",
  "water_intake",                     "Drinking",             "Daily water intake",
  "water_duration",                   "Drinking",             "Daily drinking duration",
  "water_visits",                     "Drinking",             "Daily drinking visits",
  "total_meals",                      "Meal patterns",        "Total meals",
  "median_meal_duration",             "Meal patterns",        "Median meal duration",
  "median_visit_per_meal",            "Meal patterns",        "Median visits per meal",
  "median_intake_per_meal",           "Meal patterns",        "Median intake per meal",
  "median_feeding_pct_per_meal",      "Meal patterns",        "Median feeding % per meal",
  "number_of_non_nutritive_visits",   "Non-nutritive behavior", "Non-nutritive visits",
  "median_non_nutritive_per_meal",    "Non-nutritive behavior", "Median non-nutritive per meal",
  "total_actor",                      "Social dominance",     "Total actor events",
  "total_reactor",                    "Social dominance",     "Total reactor events"
)

tbl1_dat <- rep %>%
  select(variable,
         R_cow_mean, R_cow_lower, R_cow_upper,
         CVi_mean, CVi_lower, CVi_upper) %>%
  inner_join(
    pred %>% select(variable,
                    CVP_mean, CVP_lower, CVP_upper,
                    rIIV_mean, rIIV_lower, rIIV_upper),
    by = "variable"
  ) %>%
  inner_join(var_meta, by = "variable") %>%
  mutate(
    Category = factor(Category, levels = c(
      "Feeding", "Drinking", "Meal patterns",
      "Non-nutritive behavior", "Social dominance"
    )),
    R    = fmt_ci(R_cow_mean, R_cow_lower, R_cow_upper),
    CVi  = fmt_ci(CVi_mean,   CVi_lower,   CVi_upper),
    CVP  = fmt_ci(CVP_mean,   CVP_lower,   CVP_upper),
    rIIV = fmt_ci(rIIV_mean,  rIIV_lower,  rIIV_upper)
  ) %>%
  arrange(Category) %>%
  select(Category, Variable,
         R, R_mean = R_cow_mean,
         CVi,  CVi_mean,
         CVp  = CVP,  CVP_mean,

# Build per-column gradient fills based on the posterior mean
make_fills <- function(values, low, high) {
  pal <- scales::col_numeric(c(low, high), domain = range(values, na.rm = TRUE))
  pal(values)
}
fill_R    <- make_fills(tbl1_dat$R_mean,    "#E8F5E9", "#1B5E20")  # greens
fill_CVi  <- make_fills(tbl1_dat$CVi_mean,  "#E3E8F5", "#1A237E")  # blues
fill_CVP  <- make_fills(tbl1_dat$CVP_mean,  "#FFF3E0", "#BF360C")  # oranges
fill_rIIV <- make_fills(tbl1_dat$rIIV_mean, "#F3E5F5", "#4A148C")  # purples

# Pick black/white text for contrast against a hex fill
pick_text_color <- function(hex) {
  rgb <- grDevices::col2rgb(hex)
  lum <- (0.299 * rgb[1, ] + 0.587 * rgb[2, ] + 0.114 * rgb[3, ]) / 255
  ifelse(lum > 0.6, "#000000", "#FFFFFF")
}

tbl1_disp <- tbl1_dat %>%
  transmute(Category, Variable, R, CVi, CVP = CVp, rIIV)

ft <- flextable(tbl1_disp) %>%
  set_header_labels(
    R    = "R [95% CI]",
    CVi  = "CVi [95% CI]",
    CVP  = "CVP [95% CI]",
    rIIV = "rIIV [95% CI]"
  ) %>%
  merge_v(j = "Category") %>%
  theme_booktabs() %>%
  align(j = "Variable", align = "left",   part = "body") %>%
  align(j = c("R","CVi","CVP","rIIV"), align = "center", part = "body") %>%
  align(align = "center", part = "header") %>%
  valign(j = "Category", valign = "top", part = "body") %>%
  bold(j = "Category", part = "body") %>%
  bg(bg = "#1F3A93", part = "header") %>%
  color(color = "white", part = "header") %>%
  bold(part = "header")

# Apply per-row gradient fills (flextable renders these natively in docx)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(tbl1_disp))) {
  ft <- ft %>%
    bg(i = i, j = "R",    bg = fill_R[i]) %>%
    color(i = i, j = "R",    color = pick_text_color(fill_R[i])) %>%
    bg(i = i, j = "CVi",  bg = fill_CVi[i]) %>%
    color(i = i, j = "CVi",  color = pick_text_color(fill_CVi[i])) %>%
    bg(i = i, j = "CVP",  bg = fill_CVP[i]) %>%
    color(i = i, j = "CVP",  color = pick_text_color(fill_CVP[i])) %>%
    bg(i = i, j = "rIIV", bg = fill_rIIV[i]) %>%
    color(i = i, j = "rIIV", color = pick_text_color(fill_rIIV[i]))
}

ft <- ft %>%
  fontsize(size = 9, part = "all") %>%
  autofit()

ft

## 4.2 Within-Individual Variation: Predictability

We use the coefficient of variation of predictability (CVP) as the primary metric for cross-trait comparisons of predictability, and report rIIV alongside to provide a biological anchor for these values: it expresses how many times more variable the least-predictable cows are compared to the most-predictable cows.

Variables related to meal-patterns were the most predictable. The median number of non-nutritive visits per meal (CVP = `r cvp_val("median_non_nutritive_per_meal")` `r cvp_ci("median_non_nutritive_per_meal")`; rIIV = `r riiv_val("median_non_nutritive_per_meal")` `r riiv_ci("median_non_nutritive_per_meal")`), median visits per meal (CVP = `r cvp_val("median_visit_per_meal")` `r cvp_ci("median_visit_per_meal")`; rIIV = `r riiv_val("median_visit_per_meal")` `r riiv_ci("median_visit_per_meal")`), and median meal duration (CVP = `r cvp_val("median_meal_duration")` `r cvp_ci("median_meal_duration")`; rIIV = `r riiv_val("median_meal_duration")` `r riiv_ci("median_meal_duration")`) had the lowest CVP values, meaning individual cows expressed these behaviors at a similar level of behvioral consistency within themselves aross different days, and cows differed little from one another in how predictable they were. The corresponding rIIV values indicate that the least-predictable cows showed only about 1.2 times more variable than most-predictable cows for these behaviors. In contrast, daily feed intake (CVP = `r cvp_val("feed_intake")` `r cvp_ci("feed_intake")`; rIIV = `r riiv_val("feed_intake")` `r riiv_ci("feed_intake")`), total number of actor events (CVP = `r cvp_val("total_actor")` `r cvp_ci("total_actor")`; rIIV = `r riiv_val("total_actor")` `r riiv_ci("total_actor")`), and the median percentage of meal time spent feeding (CVP = `r cvp_val("median_feeding_pct_per_meal")` `r cvp_ci("median_feeding_pct_per_meal")`; rIIV = `r riiv_val("median_feeding_pct_per_meal")` `r riiv_ci("median_feeding_pct_per_meal")`) had the highest CVP, indicating moderately higher individual variation in within-individual behaviour consistency: some cows were more consistent than others in these behaviors, with the least-predictable cows being roughly 1.5 times as more variable than the most-predictable cows. Nevertheless, all 16 variables displayed relatively low CVP and rIIV values overall. As shown in @fig-rep-cvp-scatter B, distinguishing among the 16 variables based on CVP alone is difficult, as they cluster within a narrow range of CVP ≤ 0.22.

## 4.3 Classifying Behavioral Variables

We grouped the 16 variables into 3 clusters based on their R and CVi values using K-means (@fig-rep-cvp-scatter A).

**Behavior Cluster 1 — high R, high CVi** contained `r length(c1_vars)` variables: `r paste(clean_label(c1_vars), collapse = ", ")`. Cows in this cluster differed widely from one another in their average behavioral expression, and these differences remained stable over time. In other words, each cow had a distinctive and repeatable behavioural signature. These variables are the most useful for characterising individual behavioural profiles.

**Behavior Cluster 2 — high R, low CVi** contained `r length(c2_vars)` variables: `r paste(clean_label(c2_vars), collapse = ", ")`. Individual differences were again consistent over time, but the spread of individual differences across the herd was narrow relative to the herd mean.

**Behavior Cluster 3 — low R, low CVi** contained `r length(c3_vars)` variables: `r paste(clean_label(c3_vars), collapse = ", ")`. Cows showed little variation from one another in these behaviours, and what variation did exist was inconsistent across days. This pattern suggests these behaviours are driven more by day-to-day environmental conditions (e.g., feed availability, group dynamics) than by stable individual tendencies.

## 4.4 Identifying Cow Types via PCA

We applied PCA with varimax rotation to the intercepts (average individual cow's behaviour expression) of the `r length(c1_vars)` Behavior Cluster 1 variables. `r m3_ncomp` components were retained to meet the ≥80% cumulative-variance criterion [@cangelosi2007component], together explaining `r m3_cumvar`% of the total variance (Table 2, @fig-pca-biplots). Rotated Component (RC) 1 explained the largest share of variance (`r m3_rc1`%), driven primarily by non-nutritive behavior and feeding patterns. RC2 explained `r m3_rc2`% of variance and was most strongly associated with drinking patterns. RC3 captured the remaining variance, primarily related to agonistic behavior (actor and reactor events).

K-means clustering on the `r m3_ncomp` retained rotated components after PCA, with $k$ selected by the silhouette method, identified k = `r m3_k` as the optimal number of cow clusters. The mean silhouette width of the final clustering was `r m3_sil`, indicating reasonably well-defined groupings. An interactive visualization of the `r m3_k` clusters of cows in the 3D space, colored by cluster assignment, is available at <https://www.skysheng.io/moo4feed_decoding_animal/>.

```{r cow-cluster-biology, include=FALSE}
# ── Load per-cow cluster assignments and per-cow intercept estimates ─────────
cow_clust <- read.csv(.p("results/15_pca_clustering/pca_M3_c1_int_cow_clusters.csv"))
cow_int   <- read.csv(.p("results/14_individual_traits/cow_intercepts_wide.csv"))

# Per-cluster mean RC scores and sizes (sorted by size, largest to smallest)
clust_summary <- cow_clust %>%
  dplyr::group_by(cluster) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    n   = dplyr::n(),
    RC1 = mean(RC1),
    RC2 = mean(RC2),
    RC3 = mean(RC3),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(n))

# Herd-level mean and sd for each intercept variable (for z-scores / percentiles)
num_cols  <- setdiff(names(cow_int), "cow")
herd_mean <- sapply(cow_int[, num_cols], mean, na.rm = TRUE)
herd_sd   <- sapply(cow_int[, num_cols], stats::sd, na.rm = TRUE)

# Helpers: value, z-score, and within-herd percentile for a focal cow
cow_val  <- function(cow, v) cow_int[[v]][cow_int$cow == cow]
cow_z    <- function(cow, v) round((cow_val(cow, v) - herd_mean[[v]]) / herd_sd[[v]], 2)
cow_pct  <- function(cow, v) round(mean(cow_int[[v]] <= cow_val(cow, v)) * 100)
cow_clu  <- function(cow) cow_clust$cluster[cow_clust$cow == cow]

# Named cluster IDs (by rank in size) — makes the prose robust to k-means relabeling
rank_to_cid <- clust_summary$cluster           # index 1 = largest cluster, etc.
cid_subord  <- rank_to_cid[1]                  # largest = typical/subordinate
cid_dom     <- rank_to_cid[2]                  # second largest = dominant
cid_drink   <- rank_to_cid[3]                  # third = heavy drinkers
cid_frag    <- rank_to_cid[4]                  # smallest = fragmented feeders
```

**Cow Cluster `r cid_subord` — "typical subordinate" cows (n = `r clust_summary$n[1]`, ~`r m3_pct(1)`% of the herd, the largest group).** Cows in this cluster sit near the herd average on RC1 (mean score = `r fmt(clust_summary$RC1[1])`) and slightly below average on RC2 (`r fmt(clust_summary$RC2[1])`), but score noticeably high on RC3 (`r fmt(clust_summary$RC3[1])`). These cows are replaced from feed bins (reactor events) more often than they replaced others (actor events), and have slightly low drinking activity (@fig-pca-biplots A). Cows in this cluster are the unremarkable majority of the herd: they feed, drink, and take their meals within typical ranges, but routinely yield the bin to more dominant penmates.

**Cow Cluster `r cid_drink` — "heavy drinkers" (n = `r clust_summary$n[3]`, ~`r m3_pct(3)`%).** Cows in this cluster are distinguished by a very high RC2 score (`r fmt(clust_summary$RC2[3])`), driven by both long daily drinking duration and more drinking visits per day, while showing slightly lower than herd average RC1 (`r fmt(clust_summary$RC1[3])`) and slightly higher than herd average RC3 (`r fmt(clust_summary$RC3[3])`) (@fig-pca-biplots A). These cows express substantially high drinking activity even after we controled for DIM and THI. They have relatively low feeding activity, and get replaced slightly more often than they replace others.

**Cow Cluster `r cid_frag` — "fragmented, restless feeders" (n = `r clust_summary$n[4]`, ~`r m3_pct(4)`%, the smallest group).** This small group of extreme individuals scores very high on RC1 (`r fmt(clust_summary$RC1[4])`), driven by a combination of many feed visits per day, many non-nutritive visits, and highly fragmented meals (many short visits per meal, with repeated head-in/head-out events rather than sustained feeding). RC2 (`r fmt(clust_summary$RC2[4])`) is slightly below average, and RC3 (`r fmt(clust_summary$RC3[4])`) score is very close to the herd average. These cows have relatively low drinking activity, repeatedly switch among bins in search of preferred feed, even though there is feed remaining in the bins they visited. This cluster contains only a handful of cows, it captures the behavioral tail of the distribution rather than a common type.

**Cow Cluster `r cid_dom` — "dominant" cows (n = `r clust_summary$n[2]`, ~`r m3_pct(2)`%, the second-largest group).** These cows show average RC1 (`r fmt(clust_summary$RC1[2])`) and RC2 (`r fmt(clust_summary$RC2[2])`) scores but a strongly negative RC3 score (`r fmt(clust_summary$RC3[2])`), meaning they initiate many more replacement events than they receive (@fig-pca-biplots B). Their feeding, drinking behaviors, and meal patterns are otherwise unremarkable. This cluster represents the socially dominant cows of the herd. These cows likely benefit from preferential access to feed bins.

## 4.6 Individual Cow Stories

We selected one cow from each of the 4 clusters (cows 7068, 7150, 5042, 5120) and describe their individual stories through their average behavioral expression compared to the herd. All behavioral values reported below are posterior means of each cow's behavioral type (i.e., her individual intercept from the mixed models in Section 4.1), so they represent the cow's typical day-to-day expression after accounting for DIM and THI. Percentiles are calculated within the herd on those same posterior means.

**Cow 7068 — a "typical subordinate" (Cluster `r cow_clu(7068)`).** Cow 7068 is almost never the one replacing others at the feed bin (daily actor events: `r fmt(cow_val(7068, "int_total_actor"))`, `r cow_pct(7068, "int_total_actor")`th percentile of the herd) but is very frequently replaced by others (daily reactor events: `r fmt(cow_val(7068, "int_total_reactor"))`, `r cow_pct(7068, "int_total_reactor")`th percentile). Despite routinely being replaced at the bin, she still achieves one of the highest daily feed intakes in the herd (daily feed intake: `r fmt(cow_val(7068, "int_feed_intake"))`, `r cow_pct(7068, "int_feed_intake")`th percentile). She did not maintain the high feed intake through visiting the feed bins more often. Her feeding visits per day (`r fmt(cow_val(7068, "int_feed_visits"))`, `r cow_pct(7068, "int_feed_visits")`th percentile) are actually below the herd median. She maintained high feed intake through a highly efficient feeding strategy. When she does enter a bin, she stays for a long time feeding. Her daily feeding duration is long (`r fmt(cow_val(7068, "int_feed_duration")/60, 1)` min, `r cow_pct(7068, "int_feed_duration")`th percentile), and a very high fraction of her meal time is spent with her head down actually feeding rather than waiting next to the bin (median percentage of time spent feeding per meal: `r fmt(cow_val(7068, "int_median_feeding_pct_per_meal"))`%, `r cow_pct(7068, "int_median_feeding_pct_per_meal")`th percentile). This is combined with a high median intake per meal (`r fmt(cow_val(7068, "int_median_intake_per_meal"))` kg, `r cow_pct(7068, "int_median_intake_per_meal")`th percentile). Consistent with this feeding style, her non-nutritive behavior is low (daily non-nutritive visits: `r fmt(cow_val(7068, "int_number_of_non_nutritive_visits"))`, `r cow_pct(7068, "int_number_of_non_nutritive_visits")`th percentile) and her drinking profile is unremarkable (daily drinking duration: `r fmt(cow_val(7068, "int_water_duration")/60, 1)` min, `r cow_pct(7068, "int_water_duration")`th percentile; daily drinking visits: `r fmt(cow_val(7068, "int_water_visits"))`, `r cow_pct(7068, "int_water_visits")`th percentile). In short, cow 7068 rarely wins social encounters, but she compensates by making each meal count and spending more time feeding.

**Cow 7150 — a "heavy drinker" (Cluster `r cow_clu(7150)`).** Cow 7150's daily drinking duration (`r fmt(cow_val(7150, "int_water_duration")/60, 1)` min, `r cow_pct(7150, "int_water_duration")`th percentile) and daily drinking visits (`r fmt(cow_val(7150, "int_water_visits"))`, `r cow_pct(7150, "int_water_visits")`th percentile) are the highest in the herd, which are several times higher than the herd mean. Although she visits the water bins often and for extended period of time, her daily water intake (`r fmt(cow_val(7150, "int_water_intake"))` kg, `r cow_pct(7150, "int_water_intake")`th percentile) is actually below the herd median. She simply keep returning to the drinkers throughout the day in many short bouts. Her feeding-related variables are within the normal range (feeding visits per day: `r fmt(cow_val(7150, "int_feed_visits"))`, `r cow_pct(7150, "int_feed_visits")`th percentile; median visits per meal: `r fmt(cow_val(7150, "int_median_visit_per_meal"))`, `r cow_pct(7150, "int_median_visit_per_meal")`th percentile). Similar to her drinking style, when she visits the feed bins, only a small fraction of meal time is spent actually feeding (median percentage of time spend feeding per meal: `r fmt(cow_val(7150, "int_median_feeding_pct_per_meal"))`%, `r cow_pct(7150, "int_median_feeding_pct_per_meal")`th percentile) and her median intake per meal is considerably low (`r fmt(cow_val(7150, "int_median_intake_per_meal"))` kg, `r cow_pct(7150, "int_median_intake_per_meal")`th percentile). Her non-nutritive behavior (daily non-nutritive visits: `r fmt(cow_val(7150, "int_number_of_non_nutritive_visits"))`, `r cow_pct(7150, "int_number_of_non_nutritive_visits")`th percentile; median non-nutritive per meal: `r fmt(cow_val(7150, "int_median_non_nutritive_per_meal"))`, `r cow_pct(7150, "int_median_non_nutritive_per_meal")`th percentile) is close to the herd average. Socially she initiates somewhat more replacements than the typical cow (daily actor events: `r fmt(cow_val(7150, "int_total_actor"))`, `r cow_pct(7150, "int_total_actor")`th percentile) while being replaced at a near-average rate (daily reactor events: `r fmt(cow_val(7150, "int_total_reactor"))`, `r cow_pct(7150, "int_total_reactor")`th percentile). Her daily feed intake (`r fmt(cow_val(7150, "int_feed_intake"))` kg, `r cow_pct(7150, "int_feed_intake")`th percentile) sits right at the herd median, consistent with her overall-average feeding profile. What places her in this cluster is her distinctive drinking style: many long drinking visits spread across the day.

**Cow 5042 — a "fragmented, restless feeder" (Cluster `r cow_clu(5042)`).** Cow 5042 is the most extreme individual in the herd on nearly every RC1 variable, and illustrates the fragmented-feeder profile. Her feeding visits per day (`r fmt(cow_val(5042, "int_feed_visits"))`, `r cow_pct(5042, "int_feed_visits")`th percentile), median visits per meal (`r fmt(cow_val(5042, "int_median_visit_per_meal"))`, `r cow_pct(5042, "int_median_visit_per_meal")`th percentile), daily non-nutritive visits (`r fmt(cow_val(5042, "int_number_of_non_nutritive_visits"))`, `r cow_pct(5042, "int_number_of_non_nutritive_visits")`th percentile), and median non-nutritive visits per meal (`r fmt(cow_val(5042, "int_median_non_nutritive_per_meal"))`, `r cow_pct(5042, "int_median_non_nutritive_per_meal")`th percentile) are all at or near the herd maximum. She visits bins constantly and pulls her head in and out of bins many times per meal. Although her meals are unusually long (median meal duration: `r fmt(cow_val(5042, "int_median_meal_duration")/60, 1)` min, `r cow_pct(5042, "int_median_meal_duration")`th percentile), only a tiny fraction of that time is actually spent feeding (median feeding % per meal: `r fmt(cow_val(5042, "int_median_feeding_pct_per_meal"))`%, `r cow_pct(5042, "int_median_feeding_pct_per_meal")`th percentile, essentially the lowest in the herd), meaning that on average, she spent about half of her meal time standing and waiting next to the feed bins instead of actually occupying a feed bin. Her cumulative daily feeding duration ends up low (`r fmt(cow_val(5042, "int_feed_duration")/60, 1)` min, `r cow_pct(5042, "int_feed_duration")`th percentile). Surprisingly, her daily feed intake is still high (`r fmt(cow_val(5042, "int_feed_intake"))` kg, `r cow_pct(5042, "int_feed_intake")`th percentile), and her median intake per meal is near the top of the herd (`r fmt(cow_val(5042, "int_median_intake_per_meal"))` kg, `r cow_pct(5042, "int_median_intake_per_meal")`th percentile), meaning that even during brief head-down moments she managed to consume a lot of feed. She is also highly socially active, appearing as both an actor (`r fmt(cow_val(5042, "int_total_actor"))`, `r cow_pct(5042, "int_total_actor")`th percentile) and a reactor (`r fmt(cow_val(5042, "int_total_reactor"))`, `r cow_pct(5042, "int_total_reactor")`th percentile) far more often than typical, suggesting that her fragmented feeding style is accompanied by (and possibly driven by) frequent agonistic interactions at the feeding area. Her drinking behavior is within the normal range. Her daily drinking duration (`r fmt(cow_val(5042, "int_water_duration")/60, 1)` min, `r cow_pct(5042, "int_water_duration")`th percentile) is modestly above the herd median, and she has relatively more drinking visits per day than average cow (`r fmt(cow_val(5042, "int_water_visits"))`, `r cow_pct(5042, "int_water_visits")`th percentile). Cow 5042's time at the feeding area is made up of many short, interrupted visits rather than sustained feeding. But when she manage to occupy a feed bin, she eats fast.

**Cow 5120 — a "dominant" cow (Cluster `r cow_clu(5120)`).** Cow 5120 frequently replaces herdmates from feed bins (daily actor events: `r fmt(cow_val(5120, "int_total_actor"))`, `r cow_pct(5120, "int_total_actor")`th percentile) and is almost never replaced herself (daily reactor events: `r fmt(cow_val(5120, "int_total_reactor"))`, only the `r cow_pct(5120, "int_total_reactor")`rd percentile). Her meal structure reflects the feeding style of a cow that does not have to compete for access: she takes a typical number of feeding visits per day (`r fmt(cow_val(5120, "int_feed_visits"))`, `r cow_pct(5120, "int_feed_visits")`th percentile) and spreads them into a typical number of meals (median visits per meal: `r fmt(cow_val(5120, "int_median_visit_per_meal"))`, `r cow_pct(5120, "int_median_visit_per_meal")`th percentile). Each of her meal is efficient, a moderately high fraction of meal time is spent actually occupying a feed bin (median percentage of time spent feeding per meal: `r fmt(cow_val(5120, "int_median_feeding_pct_per_meal"))`%, `r cow_pct(5120, "int_median_feeding_pct_per_meal")`th percentile), yielding an above-average median intake per meal (`r fmt(cow_val(5120, "int_median_intake_per_meal"))` kg, `r cow_pct(5120, "int_median_intake_per_meal")`th percentile) and a high daily feed intake (`r fmt(cow_val(5120, "int_feed_intake"))`, `r cow_pct(5120, "int_feed_intake")`th percentile). Her non-nutritive behavior is on the lower side (daily non-nutritive visits: `r fmt(cow_val(5120, "int_number_of_non_nutritive_visits"))`, `r cow_pct(5120, "int_number_of_non_nutritive_visits")`th percentile; median non-nutritive per meal: `r fmt(cow_val(5120, "int_median_non_nutritive_per_meal"))`, `r cow_pct(5120, "int_median_non_nutritive_per_meal")`th percentile), and her drinking profile is unremarkable (daily drinking duration: `r fmt(cow_val(5120, "int_water_duration")/60, 1)` min, `r cow_pct(5120, "int_water_duration")`th percentile; daily drinking visits: `r fmt(cow_val(5120, "int_water_visits"))`, `r cow_pct(5120, "int_water_visits")`th percentile). Cow 5120 is straightforward and efficient. When she wants to feed, she goes directly to the bin she wants, replacing whoever is there. Her feeding time is largely uninterrupted by other cows.
